title: Elara and the Dust Song
markdown:
Sunderwind Academy’s chimneys leaned against the sky like a chess set a giant had abandoned mid-game. Inside, students whispered secrets to ferns, baked courage into tarts, or—like Elara Flickerfoot—practised Advanced Dust-Whispering with a satchel clutched too tight.

A flutter started in her knees. “Just a small delivery,” she had told the gate, while crows dragged an unnecessary shadow across the stones. Her luck was less a streak than a Bermuda Triangle for good news. Sunderwind, with its peculiar talents, still felt like a beacon that had not yet noticed her.

Old Man Hemlock watched from the dust-moted stair, hands gnarled as oak. Retired, he still used what pigeons had taught him: look, don’t announce. He saw the tremor in her chest, the polite smile that did not reach.

“Just dust, Elara,” he said, voice like pebbles finding a stream. “It settles. It remembers everything.”

A pop in the Hall of Whimsical Wonders. Professor Glimmerwing, hair like borrowed starlight, smiled too tightly: the Chronometer of Contemplation was gone. Its tick had gone erratic. If it de-synced, the academy might drift in a temporal eddy. Sunset was the deadline.

Elara’s old fear arrived on time. Blame. Misfortune with her name on it. She arranged her face into practised weather.

Lumina Starfall of Cloud-Sculpting declared the air would confess. They could see disturbances. They would find it.

Elara was given errands for every department, which was a kind of exile with footsteps. Her nose for oddities took her through corners. Glimmerwing’s office smelled of ozone and leftover regret. In the library a page lifted without a draught, disturbed by a shimmer you could miss if you were trying to be impressive.

Hemlock, in a sunbeam, watched dust being nudged. “Something small,” he murmured. “Hurried. Anxious.”

Hours thinned. The Chronometer’s tick became a panicked heart. Lumina’s clouds frayed; wisps fell off like failed promises.

Professor Pumble, kindly specialist in Synchronized Sighing, asked Elara to fetch an Empathy Gem from the abandoned Bell Tower. Lumina scoffed. “Useless, Flickerfoot. Mind your dust bunnies.”

Elara went anyway, hungry to be seen as something other than unlucky. She pictured golden light, applause, a version of herself that did not trip the world. Wind worried the tower. Wood groaned. She reached. A gust, fed by the Chronometer’s bad magic, slammed the door. Bang. Trapped. The gem, slick, slipped, fell, shattered. Not her usual quiet bad luck. Public. Mortifying.

She slid down cold stone. Below, Hemlock waited, a silent weight on the right side of the day. Storm threw wind and thunder around as if it had been hired to match her mood. For a while she did nothing heroic. She sat. Rain made a long ribbon down the slit of a window. The broken gem was only wet glitter on dark. That was the pause the academy never put on a timetable: not cloud-sculpture, not errands, only a girl listening to weather until her knees stopped lying.

Then a vibration found her fingertips. The dust on the floor was not only shaking. It was singing: a low line of displacement, energy in the wrong chair. The Chronometer was not merely mis-ticking. It was resonating. Dust, being everywhere and modest, knew where.

Hemlock’s words came back. It settles. It remembers. It also felt.

She shut her eyes. Rain drummed stone. Grit rough under her cheek. Ozone and damp earth, a metallic warp on the tongue. A pressure-point in the floor, a subtle wrongness in the air: there.

Her talent was not a joke. It was misplaced things, quiet echoes, the map nobody hung on a wall.

She whispered to the dust and let the song change key. Vibrations led her down crumbling stairs with a grace she did not usually own. The Chronometer sat on a loose gargoyle, humming chaos. Air shimmered. Time tasted like static.

She reached. Cold jolt up the arm. She held. The gargoyle complained. She pulled. She went over backward onto floor that intended to stay. The gargoyle, finished, went into a brief swirl of nowhere that closed like a mouth. She had taken the retrieval first and her own skin second, which was not the errand she had been assigned and was, for once, the right one.

In the courtyard the air settled. The Chronometer’s tick found a pulse you could trust. Lumina’s clouds were a memory. She looked at Elara with respect that had to squeeze past pride, and managed it.

Later Hemlock found her by the fountain with a perfect dust bunny on her palm.

“You heard its song,” he said.

Elara nodded. The calm on her face had not been fetched from storage. The bunny was not proof of uselessness. It was a small, ordinary choir, still singing if you bothered. Her next errand, when it came, would still go sideways. She would listen first, and let the dust finish the sentence.
characters: Elara Flickerfoot (polite but unlucky errand-runner who pretends to be calmer than they are), Old Man Hemlock (a retired pigeon fancier who sees everything)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, fantastic story for curious young teens
